verdicts.trueWording: Numerals in Rules. In rules writing, we use numerals more often.
verdicts.note: Every example in the claim is verbatim in the source: 'Anyone who touches the orb regains 3 hit points'; 'The spell lasts for 1 round'; 'The attack has a range of 30 feet'; and under 'But:' - 'The two cities are fifty miles apart' and 'After winning the fight, the characters slept for six hours.' The general rule cited is Chicago 9.2 (spell out zero to one hundred). 'always' is a shade stronger than the guide's framing but the substance holds.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the absolute quantifier 'always' in 'Game quantities always take numerals' — the verifier's own note concedes it is 'a shade stronger than the guide's framing'

verdicts.trueWording: Making up towns is tricky ... a tightrope of sorts
verdicts.note: Raw page (live URL, HTTP 200). Verbatim as the opening line of section THE TOWN AND BANDITS: 'Making up towns is tricky, they are instantly identifiable to players... but making them interesting without becoming the focus of the campaign is a tightrope of sorts.' 'for a designer' is implicit in a module review, not stated.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'for a designer' — the verifier's own note says that addressee limb is 'implicit in a module review, not stated' on the page

verdicts.trueWording: the very act of having to write it, to think harder about their encounters
verdicts.note: Raw page, third paragraph: 'It can also force adventure designers, by the very act of having to write it, to think harder about their encounters.' Quote exact. Merwin's wording is the modal 'can also force' inside a 'when it's good' clause, where the claim states it flatly; the proposition itself is his.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the flat, unconditional 'forces designers to think harder' — the verifier's note records that Merwin's wording is the modal 'can also force' inside a 'when it's good' clause

verdicts.trueWording: focusing on what the characters can immediately perceive helps to ... avoid rambling boxed text
verdicts.note: Quote exact. The page hedges where the claim does not: 'helps to both A) avoid rambling boxed text and, B) quickly identify key room elements', versus the claim's 'is what keeps'. Substance of the single asserted limb is supported.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the exclusive-causal 'is what keeps the description from rambling' — the verifier's note records that 'the page hedges where the claim does not' ('helps to both A) avoid rambling boxed text and, B) quickly identify key room elements')

verdicts.trueWording: That's pretty short. Contrast it with the first room
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the 'Tangent Alert!' aside. The 2005 passage quoted (from Sons of Gruumsh, called 'a recent Forgotten Realms adventure' - the page does not date it) is indeed three sentences; the comparator is named as 1999's Return to the Keep on the Borderlands. The contraction limb is the column's own generalisation immediately above the pair - that boxed text used to be much longer than it is today - so it is asserted, not inferred; but it rests on two hand-picked passages, not a corpus measure, and 5th edition is nowhere on the page, so 'before 5th edition' is external chronology (2005 precedes 2014).
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'before 5th edition' — the verifier's note states that '5th edition is nowhere on the page' and that the contraction rests on two hand-picked passages rather than a corpus measure

verdicts.trueWording: reduce it down to one or two SIMPLE sentences

verdicts.note: CONFIRMED for the headline and three of four bracket figures. Re-measured min 8 ('Such a journey is the stuff of legend.'), max 41 (the 'Some are vortices...' sentence on p. 363), p10 11, p50 21. One convention caveat, stated visibly rather than buried: p90 re-measures at 30.9 by linear interpolation and 31 by nearest rank, so the claim's p90 30 holds only under a lower/truncating percentile method. Nothing in the appendix falls below 8 words once the run-in heads 'Spells.' and 'Portals.' are attached to their sentences, which is how the 72-sentence count is reached.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the 'p90 30' bracket figure — the verifier's note confirms only 'three of four bracket figures' and records that p90 re-measures at 30.9 (linear interpolation) or 31 (nearest rank), so 30 holds 'only under a lower/truncating percentile method'

verdicts.trueWording: singular 'settlement' twice and once; plural adds three
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED on the counting convention the claim's own method implies. Word-boundary searches for the singular return exactly 2 in SRD 5.1 and exactly 1 in SRD 5.2.1, as claimed. Both SRD 5.1 instances are plain rules nouns - selling loot on returning 'to a town or other settlement', and delivering something 'to a distant settlement'; the SRD 5.2.1 instance is the crafting-materials rule, 'in any other settlement, that chance is 25 percent'. Flag for downstream use: SRD 5.2.1 additionally carries the plural 'settlements' 3 times (spellcasting services, an area-divination spell, and a druidic locate effect), so a reader who takes 'the word' to include inflected forms would find 4, not 1; SRD 5.1 has no plural at all. The no-settlement-table limb holds: neither document contains any settlement-size table, 'hamlet' and 'metropolis' occur zero times in both, and the only table with settlement categories is the SRD 5.2.1 Spellcasting Services availability column.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the count 'the word settlement occurs... once in SRD 5.2.1' — the verifier's own FLAG records that SRD 5.2.1 carries the plural 'settlements' three further times, 'so a reader who takes the word to include inflected forms would find 4, not 1'
